heading: Background
html:
Male hypogonadism is a clinical syndrome requiring both symptoms and biochemical evidence of testosterone deficiency. Neither on its own is enough to diagnose it or to justify referral.

Typical symptoms are erectile dysfunction, lack of spontaneous / early morning erections, and reduced libido. Some men present instead with a low-impact (osteoporotic) fracture or an unexplained normocytic anaemia.

Testosterone <7 nmol/L is more often due to a secondary (gonadal or pituitary) cause. Milder deficiency (7–11 nmol/L) more often reflects non-gonadal illness or late-onset hypogonadism associated with increasing age and obesity.

Avoid investigating men who have vague symptoms during an acute, reversible illness. Testosterone falls transiently in acute illness and results taken then will mislead — wait until the man is well.

heading: Investigation
html:
Test men with suggestive symptoms — especially low libido, erectile dysfunction and loss of early morning erections.

First test — total testosterone. Brown tube, taken between 0800 and 0900h. Reference range 10–30 nmol/L. Interpret against three bands:

<7 nmol/L — androgen deficiency likely

If there is no co-existing illness, repeat in 4 weeks — fasted, 0800–0900h — and check bioavailable testosterone, LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH and ferritin.

7–11 nmol/L — equivocal

If there is no co-existing illness, repeat in 4 weeks — fasted, 0800–0900h — and check bioavailable testosterone, LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH and ferritin.

>11 nmol/L — androgen deficiency unlikely

Referral is not indicated. Look for another explanation for the symptoms.

The confirmatory panel is the same for the <7 and 7–11 groups. What differs is the action once the result is confirmed — see Who to refer.

heading: Primary care management
html:
Before referring, do the work that changes the result — and may remove the need to refer at all.

  • Confirm the result properly. A single low reading is not a diagnosis. Repeat fasted at 0800–0900h with the confirmatory panel (bioavailable testosterone, LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH, ferritin).
  • Review medication. Many drugs cause genuine androgen deficiency (see list below).
  • Address lifestyle and weight. In milder deficiency with suspected non-gonadal illness, encourage lifestyle measures and weight loss — a 5–10% reduction in weight may improve testosterone concentrations.
  • Exclude acute illness as a transient cause before acting on a low result.

Drugs that cause hypogonadal symptoms and androgen deficiency

  • Opiates, including methadone (and illicit opiates)
  • Glucocorticoids — particularly high-dose oral or parenteral
  • Anabolic or gonadal steroids
  • Alkylating / antineoplastic (chemotherapy) agents — current or recent
  • Drugs causing hyperprolactinaemia — antipsychotics, anti-emetics, some antidepressants
  • Alcohol excess and drugs of abuse (e.g. marijuana, amphetamines)
  • Anticonvulsants — carbamazepine and phenobarbitone
  • Others — e.g. ketoconazole, spironolactone

Chemotherapy, opiate and anabolic steroid effects can be particularly profound and may persist well after the drug is stopped, though they may eventually recover slowly.

heading: Who to refer
html:
Refer to endocrinology

  • Confirmed low testosterone <7 nmol/L — once illness and drug effects have been excluded.
  • Confirmed 7–11 nmol/L — only where the man is clearly symptomatic, shows no sign of clinical improvement, and illness/drug effects have been excluded.

The endocrine team accepts referrals for people with confirmed testosterone deficiency and will discuss the option of treatment. In more borderline cases a 3–6 month trial of treatment may be considered after counselling the patient on the potential benefits and risks.

heading: Who not to refer
html:
Referral is not indicated for:

  • Testosterone >11 nmol/L — androgen deficiency is unlikely.
  • A single low reading that has not been confirmed — repeat and complete the panel first.
  • Any low result taken during acute reversible illness, or with only vague symptoms — repeat when the man is well before considering referral.
  • Confirmed 7–11 nmol/L who are not clearly symptomatic, or who are improving — repeat in 6 months if symptoms persist.

heading: Treatment and shared-care monitoring
html:
Treatment is initiated and titrated by endocrinology. The endocrine team monitors for the first year and, if stable, discharges to primary care for ongoing annual monitoring. This section supports GPs continuing established treatment.

Absolute contraindications to testosterone treatment

  • Desire for fertility — fertility services guide treatment instead
  • Current prostate carcinoma
  • Breast carcinoma
  • Haematocrit >0.50
  • Elevated PSA, or a prostate lump on digital rectal examination, that has not been evaluated
  • NYHA grade 3 or 4 heart failure
  • Liver tumour
  • Hypercalcaemia
  • Nephrotic syndrome

Monitoring

  • Check FBC, PSA, lipids and LFTs before starting.
  • Baseline PSA, then monitor annually. Baseline bone density, then every 4 years.
  • Repeat monitoring at 3, 6 and 12 months after initiation, then annually.
  • Watch the haematocrit in particular to avoid polycythaemia.
  • In milder deficiency due to suspected non-gonadal illness, consider stopping treatment at 3–6 months if there has been no clinical improvement.

Counselling points — long-term cardiovascular safety is unknown; testosterone does not cause prostate cancer but may promote growth of an existing prostatic tumour; BPH symptoms may be unmasked; some studies show increased risk of venous thromboembolism, AF and fractures; and there is no guarantee erectile dysfunction will improve. The Society for Endocrinology does not recommend routine prostate cancer screening during treatment, though a baseline PSA monitored annually is usual practice.

Preparations — base gel vs injection choice on patient preference and availability; gels are often used first to assess response and tolerability.

  • Tostran 2% gel (10 mg per metered application) — apply to clean, dry abdomen or inner thighs. Usual maintenance 4 applications (40 mg) once daily; max 8 applications (80 mg) daily.
  • Testogel 16.2 mg/g sachet (40.5 mg per 2.5 g sachet) — apply to upper arms/shoulders. Usual 1 sachet (40.5 mg) once daily; max 2 sachets (81 mg) daily.
  • Testogel 16.2 mg/g pump (20.25 mg per actuation) — apply to upper arms/shoulders. Usual 2 actuations (40.5 mg) once daily; max 4 actuations (81 mg) daily.
  • Nebido (testosterone undecanoate) 1 g/4 mL deep IM — first two injections 6 weeks apart, then ~10–14 weekly, aiming for a trough at or just below the lower end of the reference range before the third injection.
  • Sustanon 250 mg IM — usually 1 mL every 3 weeks. Contains arachis oil — contraindicated in peanut or soya allergy.

Gels: not to be applied to the genital area, wash hands after application, and avoid skin-to-skin contact for about 6 hours. For gels, check testosterone 2–6 hours after the morning application, aiming for the middle of the reference range; a level >30 nmol/L needs a dose reduction (consider skin contamination of the sample).
